name: KBR

summary.text: KBR, Inc. (formerly Kellogg Brown & Root) is a Houston engineering, construction and government-services company. Brown & Root, founded in Houston in 1919, was acquired by Halliburton in 1962; M.W. Kellogg, whose origins date to 1901, came to Halliburton through its 1998 merger with Dresser Industries and was combined with Brown & Root. In December 2001 the Army selected KBR for LOGCAP III, a ten-year logistics contract that the Congressional Research Service describes as the single largest contract in Iraq, and in March 2003 the Army Corps of Engineers awarded it the no-bid Restore Iraqi Oil contract. KBR was placed in Chapter 11 in 2003 over asbestos claims, emerged in 2005, held its IPO in November 2006 and completed its separation from Halliburton on April 5, 2007. In February 2009 KBR LLC pleaded guilty to FCPA charges over Nigerian bribes. The Halliburton file on this site holds the Cheney and RIO record; this file holds the company's own history and LOGCAP.

facts.claim: KBR's SEC filings state that Brown & Root was founded in Houston in 1919, built the world's first offshore platform in 1947 and was acquired by Halliburton in 1962, and that Kellogg, which traces to a pipe-fabrication business founded in New York in 1901, was acquired by Halliburton in 1998 through its merger with Dresser Industries.
facts.quote: Kellogg was acquired by Halliburton in 1998 through its merger with Dresser Industries.

facts.claim: The Army selected KBR for the third Logistics Civil Augmentation Program contract (LOGCAP III) in December 2001, after a competition against DynCorp and Raytheon, for a ten-year term; the Congressional Research Service describes KBR's LOGCAP contract as the single largest contract in Iraq, valued at about $27 billion, and in 2010 the Army said it would continue using LOGCAP III until the December 2011 withdrawal.
facts.quote: KBR beat out DynCorp and defense giant Raytheon for the third LOGCAP contract in December 2001, this one to run 10 years.

facts.claim: At a 2009 hearing of the Commission on Wartime Contracting, the director of the Defense Contract Audit Agency testified that KBR under LOGCAP III had continually failed to seek out and track cost-efficient subcontractors, that the contract had generated $553 million in questionable billing, and that KBR was tied to the vast majority of 32 cases referred to prosecutors for possible fraud charges. These were audit findings and referrals, not convictions.
facts.quote: the LOGCAP III contract generated $553 million in questionable billing

facts.claim: In December 2003 Halliburton placed KBR and other subsidiaries into Chapter 11 as a result of a $4.2 billion asbestos settlement; KBR emerged from bankruptcy protection in 2005, completed an initial public offering on the New York Stock Exchange in November 2006, and its separation from Halliburton was completed on April 5, 2007.
facts.quote: The separation was completed on April 5, 2007

sources.title: History of Kellogg Brown & Root, Inc.

facts.claim: A federal appeals court unanimously affirmed a 2017 Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals ruling that the U.S. government had breached its contractual obligation to provide physical security to KBR in Iraq, in a dispute over KBR's use of private security subcontractors.
facts.quote: A federal appeals court unanimously affirmed a 2017 ruling by the Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals that held the United States government breached its contractual obligation to provide physical security.

openQuestions: The site's consent page gives $39.5 billion in Iraq war-related contracts to KBR; the sources reached give $27 billion for LOGCAP (CRS) and do not confirm the $39.5 billion figure, which appears to come from a 2013 Financial Times analysis that was unreachable.
KBR's own site (kbr.com) was not returned by search; the SEC 10-Ks stand in for the company's own account.
